figures.label: eq1
figures.caption: Eq. (1), PDF p.2 (printed p.204) left: σ_R = √n — in a random mixture the number of minor drug particles per sample is Poisson-distributed [7, 23]; σ_R = standard deviation, n = average number of drug particles per sample.

figures.label: p203-summary
figures.caption: p.203 left SUMMARY: Hersey's ordered mixtures imply 'ordered adhesion' (identical or almost identical number of fines per carrier); with 'random adhesion' (random variation of the number of adhering fines per diluent particle) pseudorandom mixtures at best, with the homogeneity and statistical properties of fully randomized systems; ordered (not random) adhesion required for ordered mixtures; 'So far, no mechanism has been established that may yield ordered adhesion.'

figures.label: p203-intro-random-best
figures.caption: p.203 left → right top: INTRODUCTION — earlier mixing theories dealt with free-flowing powders of similar size [1]; best possible result = random mixture = completely disordered distribution of all individual particles [2]; approximate equations by Lacey [2, 3], Buslik [4], Stange [5], Poole et al. [6] and Johnson [7].

figures.label: p203-intro-cohesion
figures.caption: p.203 right: real systems contain cohesive, interacting portions (drug–diluent mixtures [8]) → cohesion and/or adhesion give some degree of order [9]; cohesion → incomplete mixtures of poorer quality than random [10, 11]; random heterogeneity governed by the coarsest fractions → coherence of cohesive fines gives no mixing quality significantly different from random [9].

figures.label: p203-p204-hersey-concept
figures.caption: p.203 right → p.204 left top: adhesion of one component to the other may give higher than random homogeneity under certain circumstances [12]; Hersey [13, 14]: ideally ordered mixtures by complete adhesion of an identical number of equally sized fines to each coarse, homosized carrier; stimulus for studies [9, 15–19]; to what extent does this apply to real mixtures given the idealized conditions [9].

figures.label: p204-ordered-adhesion-idealization
figures.caption: p.204 left: the adhesion process must be supposed to occur in an ordered way [9]; irregular texture and energy distribution of real surfaces [20, 21] → diluent particles not equivalent in binding capacity → number of adhering fines hardly identical; even with idealized grains it is open how ordered adhesion might occur during mixing.

figures.label: p204-random-adhesion-indications
figures.caption: p.204 left: indications of random adherence — List and Müller [22]: glidants (talc, colloidal silica) do not cover the carriers uniformly but accumulate at the microcavities between the surface asperities; the physics of adhesion assumes a statistical (random) asperity distribution [20, 21].

figures.label: p204-scope
figures.caption: p.204 left: scope — homogeneity calculated for complete but random adhesion of a homosized minor ingredient (drug) to a homosized major constituent (diluent), compared with a fully randomized and an ideally ordered system; influence of the particle size distribution deferred to subsequent communications.

figures.label: p204-theory-poisson-cv
figures.caption: p.204 left bottom → right top: THEORY — random mixture → Poisson [7, 23], σ_R = √n (eqn 1); tolerance limits stated in % → CV C_R (eqn 2); C_R ∝ 1/√n and represents the weight variation if the drug particles are uniform in size (and weight).

figures.caption: p.204 right: two processing steps for random adhesion; first, mixing yields the smallest units = one carrier + an average n1 of adhering fines; their C_unit is Poissonian (eqn 3).

figures.label: p205-discussion-not-ordered
figures.caption: p.205 right DISCUSSION: adhesion does not necessarily give an ordered mixture (= higher homogeneity than a random mixture [25]); random adherence → at best the quality of a fully randomized system, even with homosized components and complete, monoparticular adhesion of the fines.

figures.label: p205-contra-yeung-hersey
figures.caption: p.205 right: contrast to the claim of Yeung and Hersey [26] ('… implies that it is possible to produce ordered mixtures of a higher magnitude of homogeneity than for random mixtures'); not adhesion per se but only ordered adhesion; cannot be excluded in exceptional cases, but no mechanism established.

figures.label: p205-random-statistics
figures.caption: p.205 right: random adhesion = the more realistic assumption [20–22]; homogeneity and statistical properties identical to random mixtures; CV inversely related to the square root of drug content and sample size; example 1 % at 0.1265 mg (one unit) → 0.1 % at 12.65 mg (100 units).

figures.label: p205-p206-conclusion
figures.caption: p.205 right → p.206 left: ordered mixtures characterized by the independence of their standard deviation from the sample size above one ordered unit (Yeung and Hersey [26]); conclusion: random-adhesion mixtures do not comply with the criteria for ordered mixtures, feature the basic characteristics of random systems but not the fully disordered pattern → 'pseudorandom mixture' [25].
